The Hemp Bounties Act, 1923, administration of act, $500.
This is a new item.

I think it would be very nice if the minister would let us know how the matter stands. This matter is of very great interest to the northwest in particular. It is hoped that under the provisions of the act-at least that is the hope of the Finance minister, and I think he had some justification for it-with the assistance that the government was giving we would be able to work up a really large industry in hemp products in Canada. At that time it was a question whether or not the work could go on and whether the mill would be installed. I am sure the House would be interested to know whether the work is going on and what position it is in, and whether the mill has been started, and so on.

Supply-Trade and Commerce

I think probably I
can explain this matter to the hon. member for West York (Sir Henry Drayton), as I am more familiar with the local situation than the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Low). Two years ago a bill was introduced to give bounties for the creation of a hemp rope and binder twine industry in Winnipeg. At that time negotiations were going on between certain people in Winnipeg and people in Ireland who were familiar with the rope, binder twine, hemp, flax and similar industries. At that time I thought the amount of the bounty was a little too small. As a matter of fact it did not interfere with the creation of the industry at that time. The real object of getting this bounty was to encourage a new industry, and at the same time to protect that industry from a possible war with the International Harvester Company in the United States, which company manufactured a great deal of similar products. However, we are taking the matter up keenly in Winnipeg now. I have been advised by the men who worked on the project that there were people in Winnipeg from the Old Land; I believe a great deal of ground is being seeded this year, and I am advised that there are fair hopes of the industry being established. Undoubtedly if it can be done it will be a wouderful thing for the western country. Growing out of this hemp, if we can supply enough binder twine there to take care in reasonable degree of the necessities of the western country, it will be a great aid to the western farmer in his work. It will also be sound policy in every way, and will afford employment there in the winter time and will keep capital, labour and money in that section of the country.
Sir HENRY' DRAYTON: Perhaps the hon. minister can go a little further than the Solicitor General (Mr. McMurray) and tell us what the real difficulties are in this matter. As I recollect it, the question turned on two issues; one was the amount and the other was the duration. I think the duration had probably more to do with it than the amount. In other words, one of the all-important questions to those behind the scheme was that they should have such condition of affairs created for them under their contract with the government that they would be able to count upon a certain number of years during which they could go on undisturbed in the advanced cultivation of flax under the agreement as it was thought that the industry might take some time to work up. I remember that at the time I thought that in some instances the contract might

prove to be unworkable and so the work would not go on. I would like really to know from my hon. friend whether the work is going on, and if not, in what particular this contract has been found to be unworkable, and for what reason the west is prevented from getting this all-important industry?

In reply to my hon.
friend, I say that this really means the addition of a new product so far as Canada is concerned. The hemp is altogether different from the flax. In western Canada it grows to a height of from eight to ten feet. We first got a knowledge of the use of it from the people -who came from Europe, and people in the Dauphin country. They were growing it and manufacturing a coarse kind of linen for their own use. We had tested it out in various places. The Winnipeg Board of Trade became interested in it. We tested it in various places around Winnipeg, and we were able to prove that it grew very well. The climate was not against it, and the product was of a high quality. The difficulty in the way of getting capital to invest in the enterprise was the fact that they were afraid of a war with the International Harvester Company, an immense institution heavily capitalized, which corporation would undoubtedly have competed strongly against us. They asked a certain bounty per pound on the finished product, and we did not give them what they wanted. If my memory is right they wanted about three and one-half cents a pound at that time, reducing each year. I think if the government accepted the principle involved, they should not stand in the way of a reasonable amount being granted to establish an industry there which apparently was indigenous to that part of the country. We grew the product and marketed it right at our door. We had electrically-turned spinning wheels in the industry and had the labour there. In every way it looked like a legitimate proposition once it got started. But we had to guard against this large organization in the United States that we felt would wage war against us. I think the government at that time having accepted the principle, should have supported it more generously, and that is really the root of the trouble. One of the leading men interested in the enterprise, a gentleman from Belfast, Ireland, after the negotiations had been running for some time, unfortunately died. He was very active in the promotion of this enterprise, and after his death other negotiations had to be opened up. I understand the bounty was good for six years at two and one-half cents a pound.

Supply-Trade and Commerce
I believe they agreed on two and one-half cents a pound. The Board of Trade in Winnipeg has taken the matter up actively. The city of Winnipeg feels that the time has come that it no longer sits at the receipt of customs in the wholesale line and that industries should be established that are indigenous to the country; and they are going actively into the question. They are in touch with this man who, as I said before, is in Winnipeg at the present time. The difficulty was purely a matter of getting a sufficient return for five or six years until they got on their feet with the industry established, and after that they would be able to meet any competition. This assistance was simply against a large combine in the United States.
I do not know whether I have answered my hon. friend fully or not, but that was the trouble. They felt that the drop of one-half cent per pound might come too early, before they were on their feet and the market was fully secured. While I am not a high protec-ionist, neither am I a free trader; but I think this was one case where an industry which was indigenous to the country and had every prospect of success was entitled to a bounty, and I think the bounty should have been a little more generous than it was. If that had been the case, the industry would have been established to-day.

It is only fair to say to my hon. friend, whether he is a protectionist or a free trader or anything else, I think at the moment he is rather more concerned as a Manitoban, to do something for his district that needs the help badly.
Always.
How badly?

Just like most parts of Canada, very much in need at the present minute. My hon. friend asks me if he has answered the question fully. He has, but not quite definitely. I think the committee ought to know what really stands between success and failure in this instance. The differences are not very great and the difference in cost to the country cannot be at all excessive. Perhaps my hon. friend is in a position to inform the committee what changes to-day in the contract will ensure the going ahead of this project?

I am glad to have my hon. friend's deep interest in this matter. He wants to know exactly what the difficulty is. The difficulty is simply the amount of
bounty that is being given. If the bounty had been four cents instead of three, I think the enterprise would have gone through with flying colours. The question is one of financing the company, and this menace was in the way. I think it costs five million dollars to establish the industry, and the people who are advancing the money will not risk five million dollars without a reasonable certainty of success.
Are these men from Ireland who are negotiating the same people who were negotiating in 1921 and 1922?

It was a Mr. Coote who was negotiating in 1921 and 1922. I do not know exactly who the present man is who is out there, but Mr. Coote was interested in the negotiations going on at the time we brought in the bill. He felt that he would have great difficulty in succeeding on account of the smallness of the bounty. Unfortunately, he died, as I said, and negotiations had to be opened up with other interests. I got a wire a few days ago stating that the other gentleman was at Halifax and was coming through.
Do I understand that the bounty at the present time is one and one-half cents a pound on the manufactured article?
It is one and one-half cents a pound on a sliding scale for the year 1926.

It is the opinion of the hon. member that this protection should be raised to three cents a pound before it will be
possible for them to go ahead?
I cannot say that I expect the protection will be raised. I have no objection to the bounty being raised and I think it is highly advisable that it should.
What is the difference between bounty and protection?

That goes into the
whole matter of education.
What acreage is being sown out there now?

I understand the seed
that is of use for this is being brought out from Italy. Italian seed is the best seed, and I think there is some pro-4 p.m. vision that it can be admitted into Canada free of duty. I do not know what acreage is being sown, but I would imagine two or three hundred acres. Of course, it will take some time to establish and build this mill. When the mill is running
Supply-Trade and Commerce

at full capacity, it is estimated that it will handle the product of 20,000 acres of land and that 3,000 hands will be employed.

Has the hemp
grown actually proved a success up to date?
Mr. MoMURRAY:	Yes: I understand
it is of the very finest quality, and the climate and soil are entirely suited for this product. It is grown all through the Red river valley, and as I said before, it originated in the neighbourhood of Dauphin among the foreign-born people.

What percentage of this
binder twine is imported from the United States?
Mr. MoMURRAY: Speaking in this House on this bill two years ago, I made the statement-I found out afterwards that I was wrong-that little or no binder twine was produced in Canada. I understand there is a large and flourishing plant at Brantford that has done exceedingly well. I would estimate, in looking over their figures, that they manufacture enough twine for a normal crop of about ten million acres. That being the case, I suppose we have in Canada crops of possibly thirty-five or forty million acres, so that I would imagine that about twenty *per cent of our twine is produced at home and about eighty per cent brought in. That is only an estimate on my part, but I do not think I am far out.
Where does the factory at Brantford get its raw material?

That is a different
material altogether from the hemp that we grow at home. I think they have plantations of their own' in Central America, and of course they get more of it from Manila.

Binder twine at present
is manufactured from sisal imported from Yucatan.

Yes.
Mr. TOiLMIE:	What would be the comparison as to cost between the hemp twine and the sisal twine?

I have not gone into
that particular aspect of the matter at all, *but apparently the men who are willing to invest their capital in Winnipeg were convinced that they could manufacture hemp twine. I understand it makes a finer and better twine than the imported article.

Might I draw the attention of the committee to the fact that if we desire to call this kind of assistance

protection, it is of a terminable nature; it is terminated in six years as against the other kind which is interminable.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
It is not an incurable
disease.

Does the minister agree
with six-year terminable protection?
I believe in assisting new industries in some form or other- always have.

I notice we are voting money under three different heads for the administration of bounties. Are three different departments, or three different staffs, engaged in this work? If so, could not the payments be administered by one staff and the vote put under one head?

There are three different acts,
but they are all administered by the same department.
The same staff?

The same staff here. Outside,
some of those engaged in the work are paid only part salary; for instance, two or three are paid 8200 in connection with the payment of bounties on petroleum and on copper.

Is there a staff which
devotes all its attention to this work?
Not at all.

How is the cost segregated for the different classes of bounties? For instance, supposing your official is dealing with copper bounties in the forenoon, crude petroleum bounties part of the afternoon, and hemp bounties the remainder of the day?

Only the outside salaries are
charged up against this vote; it does not cover the inside staff.
Will the Solicitor General clear up this point for me? Has the bounty granted to this hemp industry been sufficient to get work started?

Is there a possibility of
success on the present rate of bounty, or do those who are negotiating require an additional bounty?

I have an idea that
there should be an additional bounty; that would be my own opinion.
Will the government give it?

I cannot speak for the government. There are men in the government who are strong neither for protection nor for bounties. I think bounties are desirable for some legitimate industries, and I also think that the government, having once consented to the principle involved, should not have stood on the amount of bounty, because no bounty was to be paid until the finished product was ready, and these men are risking a large sum of money, five million dollars, in the project. I think Canada should have been prepared to assume some risk when the other people were risking so much.

In my opinion it is a very shortsighted policy on the part of the government to haggle about half a cent a pound on the finished product and about one or two years for the continuance of the bounty in the case of an industry of this kind. Mr. Coote explained to me when he was here that this industry will not only employ a large number of operatives but will also give a very profitable crop to a large number of farmers. Not only industry but agriculture is to be assisted by this project. As my hon. friend has pointed out, the market is right beside the factory practically, and the cost of transportation of the finished product will be a bagatelle compared with the freight rate from Brantford or any other centre where binder twine can be obtained. If in Manitoba flax and hemp can be produced that will make it possible for an industry comparable to the Belfast linen industry to be established there, it would be one of the best things that could be done by way of encouraging industries for the Dominion. I hope, Mr. Chairman, that the government will look at this matter in a broader spirit than they seem to have done up to the present time. I hope that if they can find men who are willing to invest $5,000,000, they will show a more generous spirit in helping those men to establish this industry and put them in a position where they can overcome the difficulties which they are sure
to meet with at the outset until they get their factory erected and in operation. Never, I believe, since I have been a member of this House have I observed a proposal against which there could be so little objection, even on the part of the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Motherwell), and, as well, of the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Low), who I believe is favourable to this particular industry-at least, having a knowledge of his good sense and sound judgment I would suppose so. I think the government ought to look at this matter in a little broader way and make it certain so far as they can that this industry will be established in Manitoba.

Judging from the statement of the Solicitor General (Mr. MeMurray) the House must be of opinion that the hemp industry is in a very precarious condition. We are asked to vote $500 for the administration of the Hemp Bounties Act, although the people who are to carry out the contract for the establishment of a hemp industry are dead, and he is looking for someone else to take their place. I think the minister had better strike out the item altogether, and wait until the company is brought into existence. I should like to say a word, too, to the Minister of Agriculture. He is a protectionist for six years. The Solicitor General wants to stretch it out, and probably would make it eight years or some other indefinite term.	.
It is terminable.
It is well to know that he is at least a six-year protectionist, and probably as he gets a little older he may add a few years more to that term.
Might I point out, this does not raise the cost of the article to the consumer.
Oh.
It does not.

Mr. Chairman, I think the
government is to be commended for resisting payment of any higher bounty. Here is an industry about to be established. According to the Solicitor General, hemp can be grown in Manitoba as cheaply as anywhere else in the world; in fact he said that it attains a growth of eight or ten feet, which shows that the soil is very favourable to the crop. The product of the factory would have its market right there at its own door, a market of at least ten or fifteen million pounds of. twine, and it has the cheapest power on the continent. And yet this industry cannot stand on its own feet. What is the use of estab-

Supply-Trade and Commerce
lishing this industry if it cannot afterwards stand on its own feet in four, five or six years? The International Harvester Company and the Brantford Twine Company will still be in competition with it. What then? The promoters will come to this government and say:	"Here is an industry that must do down unless it is protected." I am against anything of that kind any more. We have plenty of these industries established on bounties and bonuses now. The British Empire Steel Corporation is a case in point; I think they have received more during the years they have been established than the amount they have paid in wages.
How much does my hon. friend say they got?
More than ninety millions.

No, not ninety millions,
and not nineteen millions, in bounties.

It is my opinion that no
more industries of this kind, which cannot stand on their own feet, should be established. It only means a burden to the country later on, and the people have plenty of these burdens on their shoulders now.

The fact stares us
in the face that we are without an industry of this kind. We have every assurance that the country is capable of producing hemp and of producing the twine that can be manufactured from it. Experiments have been conducted and those who are engaged in the business are apparently satisfied that a success could be made of such an enterprise in this country. Yet the negotiations seem to be dragging; they are not coming to a head. The hon. member (Mr. Evans) does not want to give encouragement to any industry that cannot stand on its own feet. I could not help thinking last night as I listened to a representative from one of the Maritime provinces that this country is much greater than the people who live in it and who do not take advantage of the opportunities available to them. This gentleman pointed to the fact that over half a million people from his own province of New Brunswick are now residents of the state of Massachusetts, so I think it is about time we began to realize that there is need of our doing something to develop our natural resources.
They have been in Massachusetts for over twenty-five years.
Their numbers have increased very rapidly of late.
Not very.

What assurance have those who would like to establish an industry here that they will have a fair and reasonable chance to make a start? Minister after minister on the other side got up here last session and warned the people that this was the beginning of the end, that the death knell of protection in Canada has been sounded. Now they propose a hand-out for six years, but, they say, "look out as soon as that is used up; you can rest assured you will have to stand on your own feet then or get out." But these are not the policies that are being followed in other countries. All progressive countries are doing something to establish industries, to take care of them and to assure their success. If we can manufacture in this country the twine that we need1, and1 if that much more money can be circulated among our own pedple, it will go a long way toward overcoming the stagnation which now prevails. This is only one instance among many that might be mentioned. If the government takes some reasonable steps to do something along this line I am sure hon. members will give them every encouragement, but if it is a matter of putting an item in the estimates simply to make the people believe that something is going to be done, I do not think that is of any use. If you do not propose to do more than you are doing you might just as well cut it out and be done with it, and thus end the farce.
The remedy proposed by the leader of the delegation from the Maritime provinces yesterday was that trade should be allowed to go through its natural channels. He meant reciprocity and free trade.

At New Westminster a
cordage factory was established in connection with which all the raw materials w'ere imported. I refer to this case because of the remarks of the hon. member (Mr. Evans) who is apparently an out-and-out free trader, so much so that he would wipe off the face of the earth any industries which cannot stand against all kinds of competition, fair or unfair, principled or unprincipled.
I would not wipe them off, no.

Well, he would starve them to death. That industry was established immediately after the war, largely due to the enthusiasm of a number of returned men who put up their money to organize the business of a cordage company. After it had been established and was going with fair success, through the influence of such

Supply-Trade and Commerce
ideas as emanate from some of our friends from the prairies along the line of this wiping-out proposition, the government actually took steps to lower the duty on the finished product, to such an extent that the whole industry was in jeopardy. At that time members from British Columbia were given information which established beyond question that without a certain amount of protection against the mass production of large enterprises immediately to the south in the United States the industry would be wiped out of existence. The protective duty was increased, or rather established where it was before, and the result has been, as I understand it in a general way, that far from being an institution in difficulties the project has developed into a success and it is a credit to those who organized it and operate it. Employment is given to the people in the district, shipping is brought into the harbour by the imports of raw material, and the finished product is sold in all parts of British Columbia to the exclusion of the product from the United States.
They import their raw material from foreign countries?
Yes, they are not able to grow it in British Columbia.
Do they pay duty on it or does it come in free?

I do not think they pay duty on it; I do not see why they should if they manufacture the article here. The point raised in this discussion is extremely interesting to those from British Columbia. In our province we have essentially an industrial outlook. If we can bring into the port of Vancouver raw materials, whether they be sugar cane from distant lands to make sugar at the British Columbia sugar refinery, or materials for the manufacture of cordage brought in from Manila-
Can the raw material be grown in Canada?

Apparently it can be grown in Manitoba. It may be that the raw material will be got from that part of the country; in fact, if it is better business to use that raw material it will be substituted for the imported material. But my point is that if we in Canada are going to build up a country of economic independence, if we are not to be under servitude to the United States, we must use these instruments of protection, these methods of roundly developing our industrial life as well as our agricultural life.
For how long?
For more than six years.
What does my hon. friend mean by " economic independence "?

I will give an example.
Suppose our friends from the United States owned completely our basic industry in British Columbia, the lumber business. Let us say they owned all the forests and sawmills- everything-and sent their management in, and' after the payment of wages took all their profits which includes increase of capital making possible an extension of business, down on the other side of the line for industrial development there; I say then we should be economically dependent upon our friends on the other side. But if we owned those things ourselves through the citizens of British Columbia, and the business was conducted under their management, and the profits used for further industrial extension on this side, we would be economically independent. Although we want capital from any land, I think all experience shows that capital raised in your own country is infinitely more advantageous than imported capital, because the profits go back into your own country.

If you become economically independent of the United States, you are still dependent on production and relying on some industry in this country, which is agriculture, which is not protected at all. Is not that so?
The industry of agricultuie in Canada-and I happen to be in that industry perhaps as much as anybody in this House-is protected just as much or almost as much as any other industry.
In what way?

You get Crowsnest pass
rates; you get legislation in connection with your own business.

Does agriculture get
any tariff protection?

Any action on the part of
a legislative body which gives special rates or special advantages to any particular industry is a species of protection for that industry.

The manufacturers in
eastern Canada have advantages under the Crowsnest pass agreement as well as the western agriculturist.
Supply-Trade and Commerce

That may be so, but if you read the preamble of the agreement and the thirteen classifications of articles, you will see that the main purpose of the agreement is for the products coming from the east for the benefit of the farmer and colonization, and for the products of the farmer coming from the west for export.

It is all for the benefit of the farmer, according to my hon. friend. The manufacturers in eastern Canada, of course, are not at all interested in getting a market for their goods. They do not benefit under the agreement in any way!
The manufacturer receives a certain advantage, but I think a fair interpretation of the agreement will show that its main purpose is for the benefit of the prairie provinces and agriculture.

Does not the hon. member
know that we are still paying a higher freight rate under the Crownest pass agreement than the local rates in eastern Canada?

That depends on whether
you live in Calgary or Edmonton, but generally speaking, the rates are considerably lower.
No.

All the discussion would
indicate that it is the people who are getting the benefit of the rates who want the Crows-nest pass agreement continued. The railways, who are operating under it, do not want it.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I would draw the attention of the hon. member to the fact that his remarks are becoming slightly irrelevant to the question whether there should be a bounty granted.

I have been very much interested in this discussion. I think we are all anxious to see a binder twine factory established in the city of Winnipeg. I think, however, it would be regrettable if the impression went abroad that the negotiations collapsed because of the inadequacy of the bounties offered. I was hoping that the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Motherwell), or the member for Nelson (Mr. Bird), or perhaps the member for Dauphin (Mr. Ward), would tell us something about the actual experiences men have had in the growing of hemp. I have seen hemp grow, hundreds of acres of it. I have interviewed men such as Mr. Cotton, of Swan river valley, and I want to say that the men who have attempted to grow hemp have so far been profoundly dis-fMr. Morrison.]
appointed with the results. In conversation they have told me they cannot grow a uniform crop. I have seen patches of hemp growing on Mr. Cotton's farm eleven feet high, and other patches that would not be more than from eighteen inches to two feet -useless hemp. Furthermore, they told me that the machinery necessary to harvest it was almost prohibitory in price, that the curing of hemp was a problem that had never been thoroughly investigated, and consequently they were not persuaded in their own minds that hemp could be profitably cured in a commercial way in the province of Manitoba.

Did the hon. member
discuss this matter with Mr. Coote when he was here? Is it not a fact that Mr. Coote was thoroughly satisfied that hemp could be raised here to the greatest advantage?

I think that is just how we
get into a great manjr of our troubles. In a conversation with me-and I was very much interested in the question-Mr. Coote said that he was basing his reports upon information gleaned from certain citizens of Winnipeg, men who might be described as legitimate or illegitimate boosters. But I am speaking of hemp as I have seen it grow in the province of Manitoba, in the northern sections of the province, and of interviews with men who have had experience in growing it.

Will the hon. member
answer the question? Was not Mr. Coote, who was largely interested in this as an expert, satisfied that hemp could be profitably and successfully grown? Never mind what his researches were.

He expressed the opinion tc
me that he had little if any knowledge of growing hemp, or in fact of hemp. The Belfast Rope Works, the largest institution of its kind in the world, imports most of its raw material, and on the growing of hemp, Mr. Coote was not at all well informed, nor was he primarily interested in it. In view of the cost of the machinery, I think it will take a lot to persuade the farmers of Manitoba, particularly those who have already grown hemp, and grown it at an entire loss, that it can be profitably cured, and it will take a great deal of persuasion to get them to take up the growing of hemp in the future.
I think that this is a problem that might very well be taken up by the committee on industrial research, and we might have more information on it from the experimental farms; although I do not place much faith

Supply-Trade and Commerce
in their reports, because any hemp they have grown has been grown on small plots. I have seen it grown over one hundred acres or so, and I can assure the committee that it was not anything like uniform in height or in commercial value.

On the invitation
of the hon. member for Springfield (Mr. Hoey), I would like to give the experience of some of the experimental farms and some other farms. The very first year that I had this work in hand we sowed hemp on every experimental farm where there was any chance of its growing. You have to put it on reasonably good land, strong heavy land such as you get in the Red river valley, to attain the best success; and at our farms in both Saskatchewan and Manitoba we have had pronounced success in the growing of hemp nearly every year. In addition to that, turning away from the experimental farms I am sure that the hon. member for Portage la Prairie (Mr. Leader) and the hon. member for Dauphin are familiar with how hemp has been grown in their respective localities. One of the reasons why hemp has become so unpopular in Manitoba is this: In 1921 they grew a magnificent crop at Portage la Prairie, with the understanding that they were going to have a factory to manufacture the hemp, and that they would get a price for their product. The enterprise did not materialize, and they were left with the hemp on their hands. There was no other purpose to which it could be put, and so it was a loss. That was the condition, and they did not want their fingers burned a second time, in the same way at all events. That is the disability under which this whole enterprise has had to grow ever since 1921. The fact is that the farmers had too much faith that the money would be forthcoming to put up the necessary building and to keep it going. I think it was very unfortunate, but probably it was natural that they should go too casually into the enterprise. I have no hesitation in saying that in my opinion the heavy lands in Manitoba, Saskatchewan and Alberta are eminently adapted for growing hemp successfully, running up to eight and ten feet, and the longer it is the better the fibre will be. I saw a very large field of hemp in Hungary on one occasion and judging from the look of it our fields of hemp appear to be quite as satisfactory as theirs. Of course, I do not know how an analysis of it would turn out, but I do know that a trial shipment of hemp to Ireland resulted in a very satisfactory manufactured product. This was only after prolonged experimentation.
The experiments have been going on ,for twelve or fifteen years; it is not a new undertaking by any means. I think that the least troublesome feature of the industry is the growing of the hemp. I might supplement what has been said by my colleague (Mr. McMurray) in that regard. Just as he indicated, the reason the money was not forthcoming was because the inducements were not sufficiently strong to warrant the investment of capital in the enterprise especially during these troublesome times in Great Britain. There have been something like four governments in power in Great Britain since these negotiations were started, with the result that financial conditions are somewhat disturbed and investors will not put money into the enterprise as quickly as under normal conditions. Consequently, for the purposes of encouragement assistance must be extended, particularly during such a period as we have been passing through during the last few years. I think these are substantially the reasons why the undertaking was not proceeded with-the lack of assistance, the shyness of capital, the disturbed political conditions, all these added to the difficulty of floating bonds or any other kind of securities for the development of industries in any of the overseas Dominions. These reasons are quite understandable, and I am sure will appeal to the hon. member for Springfield.

With respect to the amount
of moisture or rainfall, does the minister think it is sufficient to grow hemp profitably year after year?

I do. The difficulty is more in the matter of weeds. You must not have a lot of weeds on summer fallowed land, because it spoils the fibre. Then you must not put in your crop too early because the cold weather in the early spring is not as harmless to the hemp as it is to wheat. Furthermore, if there is a mass of weeds at the butts of your sheaves it lessens the quality of the hemp. I have had a full discussion of the matter with the hon. member for Dauphin (Mr. Ward). I have not discussed it, I think, with the hon. member for Portage la Prairie (Mr. Leader) but I am familiar with the land around Portage la Prairie. My first experience in the west was gained there, and I think the lands are exceedingly uniform in character and that hemp can be grown very satisfactorily there; at any rate I know of no difficulties in the way. I suppose there would be some years when there would be a drought, but in particular areas, especially in Dauphin and in the Swan river country, the same amount of drought is not experienced as in,

Supply-Trade and Commerce
perhaps, the southern parts of Manitoba and Saskatchewan. I do not fear for the success of this industry because of any difficulty in the way of growing the raw material. I suppose it is like any other crop, I do not care What; even in the case of our major crop, wheat, there are occasionally off periods of production. But I do not know of any crop that is more certain than hemp if it is properly handled. But that applies also to any crop; you have to observe the conditions necessary to success if you wish to obtain the best results.

I should like to substantiate what the Minister of Agriculture has said with regard to the ability of the soil at Portage la Prairie to produce hemp fibre. I also wanted to support what the Solicitor General has said with respect to the different soils in Manitoba being aible to produce a good quality of this raw material. I was surprised that the Solicitor General did not in that connection mention the locality from which I come because it is a well known fact that if flax eleven feet high can be produced anywhere in Manitoba we can produce it two feet higher at Portage la Prairie.
I think you can.

What the Minister of
Agriculture said in regard to the experiment at Portage la Prairie in the years 1920 and 1921 is true. Flax of great length was produced there on a private farm. I believe the statement was even made that a factory was to be built at Portage la Prairie.
I should like to suggest that if the government contemplates going on with this factory it should adhere to the original proposition and locate the plant in the city of Portage la Prairie. The Solicitor General has stated that the soil of the Red river valley is adapted to the growing of hemp fibre, and that it will have a tendency to clean the ground. I do not know whether that is true or not, but I do know that the Minister of Agriculture has stated that the soil should * be absolutely clean before the hemp seed is sown. That would imply that we cannot grow hemp fibre on a soil that is dirty, it must be cleaned first. Consequently considerable time, trouble, and expense to the farmers will be entailed in cleaning up the soil and seeing that their fields are thoroughly cleaned before sowing the seed.
I should like to ask the Minister of Trade and Commerce what the attitude of the government is in the matter of bounties. Does the government wish to confine the bounty entirely to the manufacturers, or is it intended to aid also the farmers who produce their own material?

The Department of Trade and Commerce is simply carrying out the administration of the act, and if my hon. friend will address his question to the Acting Minister of Finance I am sure that hon. gentleman will be able to tell him whether he contemplates granting further encouragement to agriculture or any other industry. The matter does not come under my department. I merely want to impress upon hon. gentlemen that my department is simply administering the act.

Does it not occur to the minister that the one who produces the article in the first place is more entitled to the bounty, if any bounty is given, in preference to the middlemen who take toll out of it afterwards?

I may say that I have my own opinion about all these things, but at this particular time I do not deem it advisable to make any statement of policy. When the budget is under discussion perhaps I shall tell my hon. friend just where I stand on these matters.

I may say to the hon. member for Portage la Prairie that the producer of the hemp does share fully in the bounty that is granted. In this way: At the commencement of the industry the farmer must be paid a considerable amount for his product; I think the arrangement is that the land is rented from him and he is allowed so much per acre. He does not have to grow the hemp himself unless he wants to. The offer having been made to him the money to provide for the crop will be deposited in the bank -I think that is the arrangement-in order to take care of the farmers crop of hemp this year. In that way they benefit from the bounty. The farmer is not bound to grow that hemp fibre but it appeals to him as better, perhaps, than growing wheat, and in growing that hemp fibre he shares in the bounty.

Does the minister know
of any desire expressed by the farmers that this industry should be started at Winnipeg?
I am very sorry to say that I have not heard such an expression in this House, and I have been exceedingly astonished that I have not.
Or anywhere else?

But there has been
from the farmers in Manitoba and the Red river valley, an excellent sphere of operations. Now that the arrangements have been made

Supply-Trade and Commerce
I must say that I am absolutely astounded that our friends from Manitoba are not supporting this proposition.

The minister need scarcely be astonished. I think the reason is to be found in the fact that the farmers are not keenly interested in the matter. Two years ago I took the opportunity of sounding a representative body of farmers in my riding, and they declared themselves emphatically against it. Not 'because the country will not produce hemp; it will produce hemp and many things; it will produce apples and plums, and I believe, watermelons, in certain seasons; it certainly will produce hemp. But in the year during which hemp was tried it did not produce it very well. I have not inquired into the growing side of it, and I do not think the farmers in the Swan river valley are objecting to it so much from that point of view. I think they all believe they could grow hemp almost any season, because in the Swan river valley we have more than our share of moisture. I think that is one of the fundamental requirements in growing hemp-abundance of precipitation-and we have that in our district, to a greater degree than have Dauphin or Portage la Prairie. If there is one place in the west where hemp should be sucessful it is in the Swan river valley. We have the rainfall and we have the soil; the farmers are not objecting to it from that point of view, but they believe it would interfere with their ordinary farming operations. They do not believe the season in the fall is suitable for the curing process. And that leads me to make the remark that I do not believe the proposition has been sufficiently investigated. I do not believe our Department of Agriculture has carried its investigation far enough to justify them in attempting to bonus the industry. Before attempting to set an industry on its feet it ought to be ascertained whether it has any feet to stand on, and I am not sure, and the farmers in my district are not sure, whether the industry will be a paying one from the point of view of the farmer; and I think that when you attempt to establish an industry in the west it is the producer who should be considered. It seems to me that without sufficient investigation along those lines the possibility is that you are going to have an industry established in Winnipeg which will have to import its raw material. I can quite conceive that Mr. Coote and others were not very deeply interested in whether Manitoba produces hemp or not; it was the establishment of the industry that was a point of interest to them. Once
established it would not matter whether Manitoba could produce hemp or not, because hemp could be imported, and the manufactured article couild be produced under protection, which of course would be the natural result. I have no real objection to a bonus in principle; I think perhaps some day we will have arrived at a state of social and economic enlightenment in this country when we will sufficiently trust each other to be able to make these concessions in order that legitimate and indigenous industries may get on their feet. But at the present time I am almost sure, after hearing the expressions of opinion from this corner of the House, that this is a back door attempt to strangle the free trade opinion of the west by means of hempen rope.

I may say that my attention was first drawn to the advisability of entering into this proposal by four Progressive members sitting right over there, and if I am challenged I will name them, but I am not going to mention the names unless I am asked.
You must not do that.
Name, name.

Let one of the four make the request and I will give the names. I had a good interview in my office on this subject, and I was stimulated more strongly to go into it because I thought I had somebody behind me that knew something about the capacity of Manitoba to grow hemp. I did not divulge this two years ago, because I did not want to do it at that time, but when they have shown, not only lukewarmness from the very province and the country we are trying to benefit, but a certain amount of hostility, I think I am entitled to indicate where the encouragement first came from. If any new information has been brought to their attention since then to warrant a change, let them give us the benefit of it, and a change may be made even at this stage. If I had information brought to me at the present time that warranted me in changing my mind with regard to the possible success of this enterprise, particularly with regard to growing the raw material, I would consider myself at 'liberty to make the change, but that additional information has not been put before the House; certainly none was put before me. The longer I look into the question the more I am convinced that the manufactured article can be produced from the raw material out there. I cannot think

Supply-Trade and Commerce
of one single substantial new industry which has been established in my province during the last twenty years which has not got some kind of infantile assistance from which it has been gradually weaned. Is that not the way the animal and human kingdom is developed from infancy? But on the other hand, while I believe in helping them while they are young, I do not believe in helping them when they become hoary-whiskered and fifty years of age. I think we have been reasonable in this connection; we assist the young industries but we draw the line at the older ones. There is nothing inconsistent in our position in that respect. Would you extend the same paternal care to a young man of twenty-five as you would to a child of a year old? Certainly not. Neither should you extend the same assistance to an industry which has been in existence for twenty-five years as you would to one which has just been bom; there would be no logic in that. However, I have stated the position we take on this question. If you want to start a home industry without some assistance and let them depend upon foreign nations for their raw supplies for all time to come, well and good.
In view of the hon. minister's embarrassment-

No embarrassment
at all.
-and a non-appreciative audience from Manitoba, may I ask him if he will not place this five-million-dollar industry in the city of Vancouver, which has both arms open to him?
I made the statement two years ago that I had no doubt that if this industry was once established it would extend to the Pacific coast.
If our friends in Manitoba want to choke the industry by not supplying the hemp, we can get it by water from across the seas.

I do not think our Manitoba friends in their hearts are against it, but I will tell you what they do not like; when they are endeavouring in their hearts to assist a legitimate industry, they do not like to have it thrust in their faces that it is protection.

That leads me to the further question, what is the policy of the minister in this connection? Research with a view to an improvement in the milling qualities of our grain is of very great importance to the farmers of this country. I should like to make a short quotation in this connection from the Canadian Milling and Grain Journal, which expresses this idea:
There is little doubt that on the grain exchanges of the future, glutenin will play an important role; it will not be sufficient for a grade of wheat to bear a general good name for strength; each shipment will have to undergo its own test, and will be marketed on the basis of actual and not accredited strength.
I should like also to make a short quotation from the report of the Royal Grain Inquiry Commission. Dealing with this matter of research, the chairman states:
We are impressed with the great need for research work to be carried on for the promotion of our grain growing and milling industries. The keeping up nf the quality of wheat alone is of immense importance. Our excellent position in the better export markets of the world can be held only if we guard the quality of our grades. Commissioner Rutherford reported that in the Old Country extensive provision has been made for carrying on investigation and research in connection with wheats, flour and milling, with special attention given to the content and quality of gluten.
When we were in the United States, we visited two well-equipped laboratories for carrying on investigations in respect to wheats and milling, viz.-at Minneapolis, where the state has a 125 barrel mill and other splendid facilities, and at Manhattan, Kansas, where the state has made excellent provision for carrying on investigations in respect to questions relating to wheats, milling, baking and flours.
Canada is now in the position of being not only the largest exporter of wheat, but the largest exporter of the world's " best " hard wheat.
In the light of these facts it is very difficult for the people who are growing wheat to understand the attitude of the minister and of the government on this question. Here is Canada the largest exporter of wheat in the world, and all we are doing in grain re-

search is being done in a little bit of a one-horse place somewhere down a back lane, with only one man carrying on research. I think that is a policy this government should be ashamed of, and especially in view of the following figures:	I know the minister corrected me last year when I pointed out the revenue and expenditure in connection with the Grain Act, but I find that the figures this year are as follows: Revenue, $2,850,527.28; expenditure, $1,549,681.00, leaving a balance of $1,300,846.28. In the face of what the department has obtained from the administration of the Grain Act in the shape of weighing and inspection charges, and so on, it is not too much to ask that we should have a little money spent in determining the milling value of the most important commodity in this country to-day. I would therefore ask the minister and the other members of the government-and I am glad to see the Prime Minister in his seat- to pay attention to this important matter and extend this research work. I know it has been stated that this work is not on a commercial basis, that it is only a matter of experiment. But why not follow the example of the United States, and we export more wheat than they do, and provide sufficient testing machinery to enable these experiments to be carried out on a commercial basis. I would ask the government to pay attention to this phase of the subject.

friend that this is a very important matter. I also agree with him as to the importance of the industry. The premiums paid for wheat containing certain percentage of protein vary from time to time with the supply and demand as does the general level of prices. Speaking in a very general way, wheat containing 11 per cent of protein might be considered standard. If it contained 12 per cent protein, the one per cent additional protein might command 5 cents premium. If it contained 13 per cent protein, the 2 per cent additional protein above 11 might command 10 cents premium. For every one-tenth of one per cent of protein contained above 13 per cent an additional premium of one cent per bushel is generally paid; that is, wheat containing 16 per cent protein would command 30 cents premium over the 13 per cent protein.
I now read an extract from another letter received from the United States:
Laboratories to perform this service have been established by private concerns, boards of trade and in one instance by a state grain inspection department. Charges for making these tests range from 65 cents to $1. (In Kansas, Missouri, the laboratories can make 3,000 tests per day).
I wish hon. members to mark that statement because the time occupied in the making of the tests has been one great obstacle that has stood in the way of this reform which has been desired by our western farmers for, I think I may say, ten or twelve years at least. The extract continues:

I want to give one concrete example of the possible value in dollars and cents of that kind of work to the grain growers of western Canada. A farmer in my constituency took two samples of the grain from his crop of the year before last, the appearance of which led him to believe that that grain varied in quality. He sent the two samples to the inspection department at Winnipeg and they both graded exactly alike, No. 3 northern. When he shipped his main crop, two carloads, one of each kind, the sample test proved correct; it was graded by the inspection department as No. 3 throughout. Shortly afterwards he was visiting in Minneapolis and he took two 5-pound samples of each of the grains that he considered to be different in quality, both of which had graded the same in Winnipeg,-No. 3 northern. He approached a grain firm in Minneapolis and submitted the samples, and one of the samples was graded as No. 1 dark northern spring.

The other, they said, was worth a premium on account of its protein content. By the way, I questioned him with regard to this test and he said it was almost a matter of minutes- a matter of hours, at the outside-because it was all done one afternoon. For this second sample, which had been graded in Winnipeg as No. 3, they made him an offer of 26 cents a bushel for carload lots delivered on the market in Minneapolis. To prove that the two 5-pound samples graded the same in Winnipeg he took them back to Winnipeg on his return and again submitted them to the inspection department there, and again they were graded No. 3 northern, both exactly the same. It is such knowledge as that, gained from practical experience, that has led the farmers of western Canada to believe that there is a better system of grading than that which we have had for many years past. And if there is a better system of grading it is apparent to us that it has to come through testing. Not that grading can be improved on the basis of the mere looks of the grain; the outward appearance is often deceiving. It is only by proper testing that the real value of grain can be determined. I maintain that a lead should be taken by the department along this line. The argument has been presented here to-night, and I think effectively, that the farmers are paying for that service and that they deserve the best service it is possible to give. I appeal to the minister therefore, not to close the laboratory at Winnipeg or even to keep it practically closed, as at present, letting a whole season pass by without any particular benefit accruing from it. I would urge upon the minister that it should be put into full operation at the earliest possible moment.

The minister's practice scarcely tallies with his professions in regard to this work. Here we have practically nothing done for four years, yet it is work that means millions of dollars to the farmers. We have got the impression that the policy of the department is to leave the farmers at the mercy of the millers and the grain men.

I assure my hon. friend that

I wish to refer to another matter, the testing of our wheat for moisture. The way this has been carried on in the past has worked a very great hardship on some of the farmers. I saw a certificate for one car that had been graded No. 3 tough at Edmonton; it went on to Winnipeg and apparently they did not know it had been graded, and it was graded 3 straight there. Hon. members will know what it would have cost that man if he had not got a new grade on that car at Winnipeg. He would have lost the difference between tough and straight wheat which would have been anything from eight to twelve cents a bushel. If the testing apparatus we have in our grain inspection office to-day is not very carefully handled, it may show either too much moisture or too little moisture; it may show more than there is in the grain. If the heat is left on

The moisture content for wheat, so far as I understand it, is not fixed in the Canada Grain Act; it is set by Mr. Serls as 14 per cent, and anything more than that is graded tough. One other point I wish to bring to the attention of the minister is the practice that seems to me has just recently been put into effect at Calgary. But recently a car of wheat was shipped to Vancouver, graded No. 4 at Calgary, and the commission man in Calgary asked for a survey board to survey the sample. That board confirmed the inspector's judgment and said it was No. 4. Then the owner of the wheat asked for a re-inspection at Vancouver. Mr. Hill said he had instructions from Mr. Serls that after these cars were surveyed they should not be re-inspected at Vancouver. I took the matter up with him myself, and at my request he wired Vancouver asking them to re-inspect this particular car. When it got to Vancouver the elevator agent there put it in a special bin and wired Serls for instructions as to whether he could re-inspect that car on unloading. Serls told him no, they could not, that the survey on the car was final. party was deprived of the privilege of having that car re-inspected when unloaded. I hope the minister will act on this last request of mine. The question raised by the hon. member for Maoleod with regard to the grading of tough grain, or the tough grading of grain, perhaps I should say, is one in respect to which the farmers in the northeast part of Saskatchewan have a standing grievance. Every second or third' year we have a rainy season and our grain is more or less damp. The farmer does not complain of the grading as tough of grain that actually is tough, but the elevator companies have a habit of grading everything tough in that particular district. I have been told frankly by travellers for the elevator companies on more than one occasion that they have instructed all buyers to buy everything as tough regardless of what the grain may be in that particular district. In some cases grain which is carried over from the year before, and which is perfectly dry, is graded as tough, though the buyers themselves admit quite frankly that it was not tough. That condition of affairs has been going on there for many years. I do not know just where the responsibility of the department would come in, but the matter should be dealt with in some way. The fall of 1921 was a very wet one, and practically everything in the way of oats and most of the wheat grown in the part of Saskatchewan in which I live was graded tough. Some of the oa.ts, in fact, soM as low as 12 cents a bushel. The farmers lost hundreds of thousands of dollars that year that I consider we had no right to lose. I remember one case of a farmer showing me some oats that had been grown the year before and that was graded tough. I sent a sample down to the grader at Winnipeg and it was graded straight there, but in discussing the matter with the elevator man I was told that he had been instructed to buy everything tough in that particular district. I came down here in the early winter of 1922 and I had an opportunity of discussing this
with the Board of Grain Commissioners. They told me they had Dr. Birchard conddct a series of tests, and I have here a copy of at least part of Dr. Birchard's report, dated February 1922. It says:
The data acquired at Winnipeg, Tort William and Montreal, lead to the conclusion that the moisture limit for oats is somewhere between 14.0 per cent as a minimum and 14.5 per cent as a maximum. That is to say, the evidence appears sufficient to indicate that oats carrying 14.5 per cent moisture may heat or otherwise go out of condition under extreme conditions, but that they will safely carry under the same conditions 14.0 per cent of moisture. No evidence of heating was obtained in any car where the original moisture was 14.0 per cent or under.
My grievance is that this report of Dr. Birchard was never put into effect, so far as I have been able to find out, by the graders. In fact, I understand they have been grading as tough anything up to 13 per cent in oats and about 14 per cent in wheat. I believe that the examinations would show no wheat spoiling at less than 15 or 15.5 per cent of moisture. During the last year or two we have had comparatively dry seasons and the farmers have not had such a grievance in that regard, but any fall may be unusually wet, in which event this thing will recur and hundreds of thousands of dollars will be lost to the farmers. I think something should be done about it.
Now, the point that has been raised this evening with regard to the milling value of wheat is an old one. It has been discussed in the prairies since 1907 or 1908, I believe, when tests were made which indicated that very often No. 3 wheat would show a higher milling value than No. 1 or No. 2. In these cases the farmer lost a great deal of money. In the fall of 1911 I took two samples of my own wheat to a local miller to have them thoroughly tested. Some of my wheat was threshed before there was any rain and it was perfectly dry, not bleached in any way. It graded No. 2. Some of the wheat that was threshed after the rain and was slightly bleached was graded No. 3. I am not sure what the spread was in the price, but I believe it was 7 or 8 cents. I took samples of both these grades of wheat to a local miller and had them both ground into flour. The miller told me that there was not a particle of difference either in the quality or in the quantity of the flour obtained from these samples. It was perfectly plain that both made exactly the same quality and quantity of flour. It simply meant that the miller who eventually bought it-

This year there have been a good many complaints. We have heard a good many complaints in this House this evening, about the grading of grain. The farmers throughout the prairies seem to have the suspicion that the grading this year had some connection with the wheat pool; in other words, they seemed to have the opinion that there was a determined effort made on the part of the grain companies to put the pool in a false position. I was told very frequently by grain men that when they were expecting wheat to be shipped to the pool they had no margin; they were paid handling charges only and had no profit, so in order to play safe they graded what they call very close. If there is anything in that, it is a very serious thing, and it would be well for the government to look into it.

They were sent to Professor Harcourt under numbers so that he could have no means of finding out how the samples were graded by the inspection department. His report was that there was very little difference in the milling and baking values of any of them. I will just quote what he says in that regard:
The conclusion reached was that there did not appear to be much difference in the value of the different grades of wheat. Even the feed sample proved by no means useless for bread-making purposes, either in yield or quality; the only thing that rendered it less available for bakers' use was its darker colour. All who saw the loaves were surprised at the quality of this bread.
I may say that I myself ate some bread made from what was considered to be a very low grade of wheat-wheat that was badly frozen and which, up to that time, I had always considered utterly unfit for flour. I always wondered where all this feed wheat went, but after having tasted it I formed a pretty good idea because it yields very excellent flour. Now the results of the Harcourt tests were so astonishing that the territorial government made an extra test, which demonstrated conclusively that the first test was correct, and that there was no very real difference in the quality of the flour as be-, tween the No. 1 and the other grades. I think that is a very important thing. I should like to impress upon the minister that the department should look carefully into the matter and see if it is not possible to work a statement of that kind into the new grain act.

I do not doubt at all the statements of my hon. friend, but an experience of about twenty-five years rather convinces me that you do not get the same yield out of No. 3 that you do out of No. 1. In the

case of No. 3 you get a greater quantity of the by-products. The quality, perhaps, of flour from No. 3 might be just as good as that from No. 1, but you would not get the same yield of flour, consequently No. 3 would not be worth as much as No. 1. Speaking from a milling standpoint it has been our experience that it is more profitable to buy the higher grades-we get a greater yield and we have less by-products. We find that when you get down below No. 3 a greater quantity is needed to make a barrel of flour although the cost of manufacturing the flour is just as great in the case of the lower grade as it is in that of the higher.

Perhaps the minister's experience is not quite the same as it would be if he were buying direct from the market. I am inclined to think that some of these grades are doctored a little before they reach the millers. Now the tests carried on by Professor Harcourt in 1904 showed that in the case of No. 1 hard the amount of flour obtained was 70.S per cent, as against 68 per cent from the No. 4 grade. This difference is certainly not sufficient to account for the difference in price between No. 1 hard and No. 4.

I should just like to explain, in reply to the question asked by the hon. member for Kingston (Mr. Ross) as to whether any experiments were now being carried on by the laboratory, that Dr. Birchard was kind enough to make baking tests from the different grades of wheat and to send them to the farmers' convention at Calgary this year to demonstrate to the farmers exactly the kind of bread that could be produced from these different grades. I should like now to express publicly our appreciation of Dr. Birchard's kindness in making those tests. Of course we wired the department at Ottawa first and asked that permission be given Dr. Birchard to carry out these tests. The department wired Dr. Birchard the necessary authority but in its telegram to me stated that it would assume no responsibility for any misapprehensions that might be caused by the use of the different breads. The bread that was exhibited was from Nos. 1, 2, 3, 4 and 5. The bread made from No. 5 looked to me to be good enough for anybody to eat, and to the ordinary layman it was hard to detect any difference in the quality of bread made from No. 4 wheat and that made from No. 1. Some bakers were called in to examine the bread and they pronounced it to be first class. Their

Supply-Trade and Commerce
opinion was that it would be impossible for anybody to tell any difference whatever between the bread made from No. 4, and that made from either Nos. 1. 2 or 3. So I think that as a rule any one of our Nos. 1, 2, 3 and 4 grades, if secured as they come through the hands of the inspector and before they go through the terminal elevator, will make the very best bread.

Speaking again from experience I find that a blend of Nos. 1, 2 and 3 very often makes a better loaf of bread than straight No. 1. I should just say to the members here to-night that there has never been a complaint brought to my notice to which I have not given my personal attention at once.
